prompt: We store product descriptions in Postgres and want 'find me similar products' without standing up new infrastructure.
response:
# Similar-Product Search in Postgres (No New Services)

You have a gradient of options from "zero extensions" to "one `CREATE EXTENSION`." All run inside the Postgres you already operate.

---

## Option 1 — Full-Text Search (zero extensions)

Best when similarity ≈ "shares a lot of the same words." Great for a v0.

```sql
-- One-time: add a GIN-indexed tsvector column
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN search_tsv tsvector
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
    to_tsvector('english', coalesce(description, ''))
  ) STORED;

CREATE INDEX idx_products_tsv ON products USING gin(search_tsv);

-- Query: "waterproof running shoes with cushioning"
SELECT id, title, description,
       ts_rank(search_tsv, query) AS rank
FROM   products,
       websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1) AS query
WHERE  search_tsv @@ query
ORDER  BY rank DESC
LIMIT  20;
```

**Pros:** zero new dependencies, millisecond queries, explainable.
**Cons:** no semantic understanding. "Running shoes" won't match "sneakers for jogging."

---

## Option 2 — Trigram Similarity (built-in `pg_trgm`)

Good for fuzzy/typo-tolerant matching on titles and short descriptions.

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;   -- ships with every Postgres install

CREATE INDEX idx_products_title_trgm
  ON products USING gin(title gin_trgm_ops);

SELECT id, title, similarity(title, $1) AS sim
FROM   products
WHERE  similarity(title, $1) > 0.3
ORDER  BY sim DESC
LIMIT  20;
```

**Pros:** catches near-duplicates, spelling variants.
**Cons:** still lexical, not semantic.

---

## Option 3 — Embeddings + `pgvector` (recommended for "real" similarity)

This is the workhorse. One extension, no new service.

### Schema

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;   -- install once per cluster

ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN embedding vector(384);  -- 384-d for all-MiniLM-L6-v2, 1536 for OpenAI

-- IVFFlat is the default; HNSW is better for small/medium sets
CREATE INDEX idx_products_embedding ON products
  USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);
```

### Generating embeddings (outside Postgres)

You need *something* to turn text → floats. Options, in order of added infra:

| Approach | New infra? | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| OpenAI / Cohere / local API call from your app | No (just an HTTP call) | Easiest; per-token cost |
| Run a small model in-process (`sentence-transformers`, ONNX Runtime) | No extra *service*, but a Python/Node dependency | Free at scale, ~50 ms/call on CPU |
| Postgres `pgai` / `plv8` + a model file | None (all in-DB) | Niche; fine for small catalogs |

### Writing the embedding

```python
# app side – called on product create/update
import numpy as np, psycopg

def upsert_product(conn, pid: int, title: str, description: str):
    text = f"{title}. {description}"
    emb  = embed(text)          # your chosen embedder → list[float]
    conn.execute("""
        INSERT INTO products (id, title, description, embedding)
        VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s)
        ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE
          SET title = EXCLUDED.title,
              description = EXCLUDED.description,
              embedding = EXCLUDED.embedding
    """, (pid, title, description, np.array(emb, dtype=np.float32)))
```

### Query: cosine-similarity top-k

```sql
SELECT id, title, description,
       1 - (embedding <=> $1) AS similarity   -- cosine distance → similarity
FROM   products
WHERE  embedding IS NOT NULL
ORDER  BY embedding <=> $1                      -- uses the HNSW index
LIMIT  20;
```

`<=>` is cosine distance. `<->` is L2. Use `vector_l2_ops` / `vector_ip_ops` in the index to match.

### Backfilling an existing catalog

```sql
-- Do it in batches to avoid a single massive transaction
DO $$
DECLARE
  batch  int[];
  i      record;
BEGIN
  FOR i IN
    SELECT id FROM products WHERE embedding IS NULL ORDER BY id
  LOOP
    -- Your app fetches i.id, computes embedding, updates the row.
    -- Or, if you have a UDF that calls out to an API:
    UPDATE products SET embedding = my_embed_udf(title, description)
     WHERE id = i.id;
    PERFORM pg_sleep(0.05);   -- rate-limit the embedder
  END LOOP;
END $$;
```

---

## Option 4 — Hybrid (text + vector) in one query

Combine FTS for precision with vectors for recall:

```sql
SELECT p.id, p.title,
       ts_rank(p.search_tsv, q)          AS fts_score,
       1 - (p.embedding <=> :query_emb)  AS vec_score,
       -- weighted blend; tune the 0.4/0.6 to your taste
       0.4 * ts_rank(p.search_tsv, q)
     + 0.6 * (1 - (p.embedding <=> :query_emb)) AS combined
FROM   products p,
       websearch_to_tsquery('english', :query) q
WHERE  p.search_tsv @@ q
   OR  p.embedding IS NOT NULL          -- allow pure-vector hits too
ORDER  BY combined DESC
LIMIT  20;
```

This is the pattern that most e-commerce "similar items" widgets converge on.

---

## Practical checklist

1. **Choose the embedding model first.** It's the hardest thing to change later (dimensionality is baked into the column). MiniLM-L6-v2 (384-d) is a strong free default; `text-embedding-3-small` (1536-d) if you already pay for OpenAI.
2. **Index choice:** HNSW for < ~10 M rows (faster reads, slightly more RAM); IVFFlat (`lists = sqrt(n)`) for very large tables where you want smaller indexes.
3. **`pgvector` compatibility:** needs PG 13+. If you're on 12, Option 1+2 is the pragmatic path until you upgrade.
4. **Keep descriptions clean** before embedding. Strip HTML, boilerplate ("Free shipping!"), and SEO keyword stuffing—they pollute the vector.
5. **Re-embed on description change.** Make it part of the write path, not a nightly batch (unless the catalog is millions of rows, then a queue is fine).
6. **Explainability / fallback:** log the FTS terms that matched alongside the vector hit so support can answer "why was this shown?"

---

## TL;DR

| What you want | Use |
|---|---|
| "Same words, different order" | `tsvector` + GIN |
| Fuzzy / typo-tolerant | `pg_trgm` |
| **Semantic similarity** | **embeddings + `pgvector` + HNSW** |
| Best UX | Hybrid: FTS for precision, vectors for recall, blended score |

All of it lives in the Postgres you already run. The only "new thing" is the `vector` type and index, installed with `CREATE EXTENSION pgvector;`—no new pod, no new datastore, no new SLA.

prompt: Write an async FastAPI endpoint with Pydantic request and response models and dependency injection.
response:
```python
# app/products.py
from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Annotated

from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, Query
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

# ─── Models ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

class SimilarProductsRequest(BaseModel):
    query: str = Field(min_length=3, max_length=500, description="Free-text search query.")
    limit: int = Field(default=10, ge=1, le=50)


class ProductOut(BaseModel):
    id: int
    title: str
    description: str | None
    score: float


class SimilarProductsResponse(BaseModel):
    query: str
    results: list[ProductOut]
    total: int


# ─── Dependency (simulated repository / service layer) ────────────────────────

class ProductRepository:
    """Stands in for your real data-access object (SQLAlchemy, asyncpg, etc.)."""

    async def find_similar(self, query: str, limit: int) -> list[dict]:
        # In production this hits Postgres (pgvector, tsvector, …).
        # Returning fake data so the example is self-contained.
        await _fake_db_call()
        return [
            {"id": 1, "title": f"Result 1 for '{query}'", "description": None, "score": 0.94},
            {"id": 2, "title": f"Result 2 for '{query}'", "description": "…", "score": 0.87},
            {"id": 3, "title": f"Result 3 for '{query}'", "description": None, "score": 0.81},
        ][:limit]


async def _fake_db_call() -> None:
    import asyncio
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)  # simulate I/O


def get_product_repository() -> ProductRepository:
    """FastAPI dependency – swap this for a real instance at startup."""
    return ProductRepository()


# ─── Endpoint ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

app = FastAPI()

RepoDep = Annotated[ProductRepository, Depends(get_product_repository)]


@app.post(
    "/products/similar",
    response_model=SimilarProductsResponse,
    summary="Find products similar to a free-text query",
)
async def find_similar_products(
    body: SimilarProductsRequest,
    repo: RepoDep,
) -> SimilarProductsResponse:
    if not body.query.strip():
        raise HTTPException(status_code=422, detail="Query must not be blank.")

    rows = await repo.find_similar(body.query, body.limit)

    return SimilarProductsResponse(
        query=body.query,
        results=[ProductOut(**r) for r in rows],
        total=len(rows),
    )
```

## Running it

```bash
pip install "fastapi[standard]"
uvicorn app.products:app --reload
```

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:8000/products/similar \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"query": "waterproof running shoes", "limit": 5}' | jq
```

## What each piece demonstrates

| Concern | Where |
|---|---|
| **Async endpoint** | `async def find_similar_products` – FastAPI awaits the coroutine; the event loop is never blocked. |
| **Pydantic request model** | `SimilarProductsRequest` – validated automatically (min/max length, type coercion, 422 on failure). |
| **Pydantic response model** | `SimilarProductsResponse` + `ProductOut` – enforces the shape of the JSON you return; extra keys are stripped. |
| **Dependency injection** | `get_product_repository` is injected via `Depends`. The endpoint never instantiates the repo itself – you can override it in tests (`app.dependency_overrides[get_product_repository] = …`) or swap in a cached/real instance in `lifespan`. |
| **`Annotated` style** | `RepoDep = Annotated[ProductRepository, Depends(get_product_repository)]` – the modern (FastAPI ≥ 0.95 / Pydantic ≥ 2) way to combine a type hint with a dependency, keeping the function signature clean. |
| **Error handling** | Explicit `HTTPException` for business-rule violations; Pydantic's built-in validation covers the rest. |

## Wiring a real repository later

```python
# app/main.py
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from fastapi import FastAPI
from app.products import app as products_router, get_product_repository
from app.db import AsyncProductRepo, init_engine, close_engine

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    await init_engine()
    yield
    await close_engine()

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)

# Override the stub with the real thing
app.dependency_overrides[get_product_repository] = lambda: AsyncProductRepo()

app.include_router(products_router.router, prefix="/api/v1")
```

That's the full pattern: models define the contract, the dependency abstracts the data source, and the endpoint stays a thin, testable glue layer.

prompt: Aggregate a directory of parquet files and return the top 3 rows per group.
response:
```python
# top_per_group.py
"""Aggregate a directory of Parquet files and return the top N rows per group.

Uses DuckDB to query files in-place — no full in-memory load required.

Usage:
    python top_per_group.py /data/sales/*.parquet --group-by region --order-by revenue
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import duckdb
import pyarrow as pa


def top_per_group(
    pattern: str,
    group_by: str,
    order_by: str,
    *,
    n: int = 3,
    descending: bool = True,
) -> pa.Table:
    """Read all Parquet files matching *pattern*, group, and return top N rows.

    Parameters
    ----------
    pattern : str
        Glob pattern for Parquet files, e.g. ``"/data/sales/2024/*.parquet"``.
    group_by : str
        Column to partition by.
    order_by : str
        Column to rank within each group.
    n : int, default 3
        Number of top rows to keep per group.
    descending : bool, default True
        ``True`` → largest values first; ``False`` → smallest.

    Returns
    -------
    pyarrow.Table
        Columns: [group_by, order_by, …remaining columns], one block of ≤ N rows
        per group, groups ordered alphabetically.
    """
    order = "DESC" if descending else "ASC"

    sql = f"""
        WITH ranked AS (
            SELECT *,
                   ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
                       PARTITION BY {group_by}
                       ORDER BY {order_by} {order}
                   ) AS _rn
            FROM read_parquet(?)
        )
        SELECT * EXCLUDE (_rn)
        FROM   ranked
        WHERE  _rn <= {n}
        ORDER  BY {group_by}, {order_by} {order}
    """

    con = duckdb.connect(database=":memory:", read_only=True)
    table: pa.Table = con.execute(sql, [pattern]).arrow()
    con.close()
    return table


# ─── CLI ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description="Top N rows per group across a directory of Parquet files."
    )
    parser.add_argument("pattern", help="Glob, e.g. '/data/sales/*.parquet'")
    parser.add_argument("--group-by", default="category")
    parser.add_argument("--order-by", default="revenue")
    parser.add_argument("--n", type=int, default=3)
    parser.add_argument("--ascending", action="store_true",
                        help="Rank smallest values first")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    table = top_per_group(
        args.pattern,
        args.group_by,
        args.order_by,
        n=args.n,
        descending=not args.ascending,
    )

    # Pretty-print for the terminal
    print(f"── {table.num_rows} rows × {table.num_columns} cols "
          f"(top {args.n} per {args.group_by}, by {args.order_by} "
          f"{'asc' if args.ascending else 'desc'}) ──\n")
    print(table.to_pandas().to_string(index=False))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## Example run

```bash
# 48 parquet files, ~2 M rows total
python top_per_group.py '/data/sales/2024/Q{1,2,3,4}/*.parquet' \
    --group-by region \
    --order-by revenue \
    --n 3
```

```
── 12 rows × 6 cols (top 3 per region, by revenue desc) ──

  region   revenue  units  sku            date        channel
  EMEA     48210.33   1204  SKU-8841  2024-09-14   online
  EMEA     47102.10    998  SKU-2207  2024-07-02   retail
  EMEA     44950.55    876  SKU-5510  2024-11-22   online
  LATAM    23400.12    431  SKU-3319  2024-06-18   online
  LATAM    21890.00    399  SKU-7702  2024-10-03   retail
  LATAM    19920.77    350  SKU-1140  2024-03-27   online
  NA       91230.44   2104  SKU-9902  2024-08-09   online
  NA       88450.12   1990  SKU-4451  2024-05-14   retail
  NA       85100.00   1876  SKU-6623  2024-12-01   online
  APAC     34200.90    612  SKU-7788  2024-04-20   online
  APAC     33100.55    590  SKU-1102  2024-09-30   retail
  APAC     31000.22    548  SKU-3355  2024-01-11   online
```

## How it works

```
read_parquet('/data/…/*.parquet')        ← DuckDB globs & streams files
        │
        ▼
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (                    ← window function partitions
      PARTITION BY region                by group_by, orders
      ORDER BY revenue DESC              by order_by within each group
  )
        │
        ▼
  WHERE _rn <= 3                         ← keep top N per group
        │
        ▼
  .arrow()                               ← zero-copy into a pyarrow.Table
```

**Why DuckDB over pandas?**

| Concern | DuckDB (in-process) | pandas + `pd.read_parquet` |
|---|---|---|
| Memory | Streams / columnar, only materialises the final ≤ N rows per group | Loads **all** files into RAM first |
| Speed | Vectorised C++ exec engine, no Python per-row overhead | `concat` + `sort_values` + `head` in Python |
| Globbing | Native (`read_parquet(?)`) | You write the `glob` + loop yourself |
| Dependencies | `duckdb` (single wheel, no server) | `pyarrow` + `pandas` + `pyarrow` again |

Both are pure-Python-install, no database server. DuckDB just does the scanning and windowing in compiled code.

## Swapping in your real schema

If your files have a known schema, you can also add **filters** and **aggregates** without changing the shape of the function:

```python
def top_per_group_filtered(
    pattern: str,
    group_by: str,
    order_by: str,
    *,
    n: int = 3,
    where: str | None = None,          # e.g. "date >= '2024-06-01'"
) -> pa.Table:
    where_clause = f"WHERE {where}" if where else ""

    sql = f"""
        WITH ranked AS (
            SELECT *,
                   ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
                       PARTITION BY {group_by}
                       ORDER BY {order_by} DESC
                   ) AS _rn
            FROM read_parquet(?)
            {where_clause}
        )
        SELECT * EXCLUDE (_rn)
        FROM   ranked
        WHERE  _rn <= {n}
        ORDER  BY {group_by}, {order_by} DESC
    """
    con = duckdb.connect(database=":memory:", read_only=True)
    table = con.execute(sql, [pattern]).arrow()
    con.close()
    return table
```

```python
table = top_per_group_filtered(
    "/data/sales/2024/*.parquet",
    group_by="category",
    order_by="revenue",
    n=3,
    where="channel = 'online' AND date >= '2024-06-01'",
)
```

> **Note:** the `where` / `group_by` / `order_by` strings are interpolated into SQL. In production, validate them against the actual Parquet schema (`duckdb.sql(f"DESCRIBE SELECT * FROM read_parquet('{pattern}')")`) or use parameterised identifiers to avoid injection from user-supplied values.
